Men marry because they're tired; women marry because they're curious. Both end up disappointed.”

“I don't think I'm likely to marry, Harry. I'm too much in love. That's one of your sayings. I'm following it, just as I follow everything you tell me.”

“Who are you in love with?” Lord Henry asked after a pause.

“An actress,” Dorian Gray said, blushing.

Lord Henry shrugged. “That's a rather ordinary way to begin.”

“You wouldn't say that if you saw her, Harry.”

“Who is she?”

“Her name is Sibyl Vane.”

“I've never heard of her.”

“Nobody has. But one day people will. She's a genius.”

“My dear boy, no woman is a genius. Women are meant to be decorative. They never have anything to say, but they say it beautifully. Women show the victory of the body over the mind, just as men show the victory of the mind over morals.”

“Harry, how can you say that?”

“My dear Dorian, it's perfectly true. I'm studying women at the moment, so I should know. The subject isn't as difficult as I expected. In the end, I've found only two kinds of women: plain ones and painted ones. Plain women are very useful. If you want people to think you're respectable, all you have to do is take them in to supper. The others are delightful, but they make one mistake. They put on makeup to look young. Our grandmothers put it on to help them talk brilliantly. Rouge and wit used to go together. Those days are over. Now, if a woman can look ten years younger than her own daughter, she's perfectly happy. As for conversation, only five women in London are worth talking to, and two of those can't be welcomed into respectable society. But tell me about your genius. How long have you known her?”

“Oh, Harry! Your opinions frighten me.”

“Never mind that. How long have you known her?”

“About three weeks.”

“And where did you find her?”

“I'll tell you, Harry, but you must try to understand. After all, none of it would have happened if I hadn't met you. You gave me a wild desire to learn everything about life. For days after we met, something seemed to pulse through my veins. When I sat about in the park or walked along Piccadilly, I watched everyone who passed me. I wondered with a fierce curiosity what kind of lives they lived. Some fascinated me. Others terrified me. It was as if there were a wonderful poison in the air. I longed for new sensations....

“Git up! What you up to?”

I opened my eyes and peered around, trying to figure where I was. The sun was already up, and I'd been sleeping sound. Pap stood over me, looking ugly-tempered and sick besides. He says:

“What you doing with that gun?”

I reckoned he didn't remember a thing about what he'd been up to, so I says:

“Somebody was trying to break in, and I was waiting for him.”

“Why didn't you wake me?”

“Well, I tried, but I couldn't; there wasn't no stirring you.”

“Well, that's all right. Don't spend the whole day standing there jawing. Get out and see if the lines have caught a fish for breakfast. I'll follow you in a minute.”

He unlocked the door, and I hurried up the river-bank. I saw bits of branches and such floating by, with a little scattering of bark, so I knowed the river was starting to rise. I thought what fine times I'd be having now if I was over in town. That June rise always used to bring me luck; once it starts, along comes cordwood drifting down and bits of log rafts—sometimes twelve logs stuck together. All you've got to do is catch them and sell them at the wood-yards and sawmill.

I kept going up the bank, watching for pap with one eye and for whatever the rise might bring with the other. Then, all of a sudden, here comes a canoe—a real beauty, thirteen or fourteen feet long, floating as high as a duck. I jumped head-first from the bank like a frog, clothes and everything, and swum towards her. I fully expected somebody would be lying in the bottom, because folks often played that trick, and just when a fellow had rowed his skiff nearly alongside they'd sit up and laugh at him. But this wasn't that kind. She was truly a drifting canoe, and I climbed aboard and paddled her in. The old man'll be pleased to see this, I thinks; she's worth ten dollars. But pap still wasn't anywhere in sight when I reached shore, and while I was steering into a small creek like a gulley, overhung with willows and vines, a different notion came to me. I'd hide her real well, and when I run away I'd go fifty miles or so downriver instead of taking to the woods. Then I could camp in one place for good and save myself all that hard travelling afoot.

It was mighty near the shanty, and every minute I thought I heard the old man coming. Still, I got her hidden; then I stepped out and peeped around a clump of willows, and there he was a little way down the path, aiming his gun at a bird.

“Oh, it is nothing at all! It gives me pleasure. I do not labour for money; my art is everything to me.”

Lord Arthur placed £4, 2s. 6d. upon the table, thanked the little German for his obliging assistance, and, after successfully refusing an invitation to meet several Anarchists at a meat-tea the next Saturday, left the house and made his way to the Park.

During the following two days his excitement was extreme, and at noon on Friday he drove to the Buckingham to await intelligence. Throughout the afternoon the impassive hall-porter posted telegrams from different districts of the country, announcing racing results, decisions in divorce cases, the condition of the weather, and similar matters. Meanwhile the tape delivered tiresome particulars of an all-night sitting of the House of Commons and a minor panic upon the Stock Exchange. At four the evening newspapers arrived, and Lord Arthur retired into the library carrying the Pall Mall, the St. James's, the Globe, and the Echo. This greatly enraged Colonel Goodchild, who wished to see the accounts of a speech he had made that morning at the Mansion House concerning South African Missions and the desirability of appointing black Bishops in every province, and who, for some unexplained reason, cherished a decided prejudice against the Evening News. Not one of the papers, however, made the faintest reference to Chichester, and Lord Arthur concluded that his attempt had miscarried. The disappointment was dreadful, and for a while quite robbed him of his composure. Herr Winckelkopf, whom he visited on the following day, was profuse in his apologies, offering either a second clock without charge or a case of nitro-glycerine bombs at cost. Lord Arthur, however, had ceased to trust explosives altogether, and Herr Winckelkopf himself conceded that adulteration was now so universal that one could scarcely obtain even pure dynamite. Yet the little German, though admitting that the mechanism must have suffered some fault, still entertained hopes of the clock exploding. He cited a barometer he had once dispatched to the military Governor of Odessa, which had been set to explode after ten days but had waited nearly three months. True, when it finally went off it achieved no more than blowing a housemaid to pieces, the Governor having left town six weeks earlier; but it at least demonstrated that dynamite, when directed by machinery, remained a potent destructive agent, if a somewhat tardy one.
